faqs.a: Pricing turns on the species involved, the height and condition of the roofline, and whether droppings or nesting debris need cleaning out afterward. Salem's range is wide for a small city: a marsh-edge ranch with skunks under the stoop and a Broadway Victorian with a bat colony price from different worlds, and the written quote keeps them separate. Every job starts with an inspection; you get the full figure in writing before removal or sealing begins, and nothing is quoted sight-unseen over the phone.

faqs.q: There is a dead-animal smell in my Salem house but I can't find anything — can you?
faqs.a: Yes — locating it is a method, not a guess. Smell intensity, fly activity, and the floor plan narrow it to a wall void, a crawlspace corner, or a stretch of ductwork, and we open the smallest section that lets us remove the carcass. In Salem's old houses a dead raccoon in a wall void announces itself to the whole street's worth of flies at one window; locating it by the fly pattern is faster than any amount of sniffing. The spot then gets disinfected and deodorized, and we check how the animal got in, because a carcass in a wall usually means an entry that is still open. Carcasses of rabies-vector species are handled with gloves and bagged, never bare-handed.

Salem.wildlife_intro:
Salem is a small, historic county seat on its namesake river, a few streets of colonial and Victorian brick homes, the old Fenwick-era core, and bayshore marsh opening up beyond the town's edges. The housing is old and the town is quiet, and the wildlife is correspondingly bold. Raccoons den in the chimneys and porch roofs of the historic blocks, bats hold the tall attics, rats work the older downtown basements, and groundhogs and skunks take the lots that shade into farmland and marsh. In Salem the habitat is never more than a street away.

Masonry chimneys deserve a slow look. Mortar joints crumble at the crown, flashing lifts where the stack meets the roof, and an uncapped flue reads to a raccoon like a hollow tree. Sealing here is masonry work as much as animal work: a correctly sized cap, repointed joints where they have failed, and flashing reset so water stays out along with the wildlife. Brick and stone stacks on older houses often hide a second, unused flue that nobody remembers — exactly the sort of quiet, warm shaft a denning animal chooses in March. Salem's brick chimneys include some of the oldest residential stacks in South Jersey, and cap and crown condition is reported on every inspection here as a matter of course.

faqs.q: An opossum is living under my Pennsville Township deck — should I be worried?
faqs.a: Mostly about the mess, not disease: opossums are not on New Jersey's high-risk rabies list, and they are placid, slow animals that would rather play dead than fight. The refuge-edge streets produce Pennsville's steadiest opossum traffic; the animals den under decks and commute the marsh edge nightly, and screening the deck ends the tenancy without ending the commute past the yard. They do shred insulation and vent ducts when they den in a crawlspace, so we take them out, clean up what they left, and screen the deck or crawlspace opening with buried hardware cloth. Check for young in the pouch season before assuming it is a solo tenant.

faqs.q: There is heavy thumping in my Pennsville Township attic at night — is it a raccoon?
faqs.a: Heavy, deliberate thumping after dark is the classic raccoon signature; squirrels sound lighter and keep daytime hours. Near Fort Mott and the river the thumping usually traces to a house backing onto open marsh woods, where a raccoon has a covered approach to the roof from the tree line. We locate the entry — often a pushed-up soffit or a vent the animal has peeled back — check for a litter before anything moves, and get the family out together. Because raccoons sit on New Jersey's rabies-vector list, droppings and latrine areas in the attic get treated as contaminated material, not swept aside.

Pennsville Township.wildlife_intro:
Pennsville stretches along the Delaware River under the Delaware Memorial Bridge: older postwar neighborhoods, the Fort Mott and riverfront area, Riverview Beach's shore blocks, and Supawna Meadows refuge marsh filling the township's middle. The river and the marsh run the call log. Raccoons and opossums commute out of the refuge into the crawlspaces and chimneys, skunks den under the porches of the shore blocks, groundhogs dig the field edges, and bats work the attics of the older homes. River towns get river wildlife, at scale.

Crawlspaces collect problems quietly. A vent screen rusts through, a pipe penetration was never sealed, and within a season the space underneath the house holds opossums, skunks, or a raccoon latrine — along with the odor that rides the ductwork upstairs. The fix starts with a light and a full circuit underneath: every vent screened in metal, gaps around plumbing and wiring sealed, and any carcass or waste taken out. Where moisture is part of the draw, we say so plainly, because a damp crawlspace keeps attracting animals no matter how well it is screened. Pennsville crawlspaces sit in river damp, and the screening here is specified for wet ground with the sill and joist ends checked for the softness that invites the next entry.

faqs.q: Why do animals keep getting into homes in Carneys Point Township?
faqs.a: Carneys Point Township sits in southwestern New Jersey on Delaware Bay, the state's most rural county, and the habitat in between the houses — Alloway Creek and Mannington marshes — gives wildlife food and cover a short run from rooflines, decks and crawlspaces. Sealing every entry we find, not just the obvious one, is what ends the cycle here.

faqs.q: Do groundhogs do real damage in Carneys Point Township?
faqs.a: They do in Salem County: burrows under decks, sheds and foundation edges undermine slabs and channel water against the house, and garden feeding is heavy from spring through fall. Our crew traps groundhogs at active burrows and backfills and screens the site afterward.

faqs.q: Groundhogs keep raiding my Woodstown garden — what actually works?
faqs.a: Fences alone rarely do; groundhogs climb and dig. What works is removing the animals that have claimed the yard and closing the den they commute from, which is usually under a deck, shed, or brush line rather than in the open. Woodstown gardens sit between the house and the field, and the groundhog commutes across that exact ground from a burrow in the field edge; the field edge is where the work happens. Trapping is set at the burrow mouth, and once the site is clear we backfill and screen it. A garden next to an occupied burrow is a salad bar with a commute of about ten feet.

faqs.q: Can bats be evicted from my Woodstown attic in the summer?
faqs.a: Not in midsummer. NJ Fish & Wildlife guidelines limit bat evictions to April 1 through May 14 and August 1 through October 15, because flightless pups would be trapped inside during the May 15 to July 31 maternity stretch. Woodstown's older attics hold the borough's summer colonies, and a caller in July gets the honest sequence: living spaces sealed now, exclusion in the August window, guano assessed from photographs in between. The work is exclusion only: one-way exits fitted during an open window, left in place through several mild nights, then every gap sealed once the colony has left. Bats are never trapped or killed — they are protected under the state's Endangered and Nongame Species Conservation Act.

Woodstown.wildlife_intro:
Woodstown is a small historic borough completely surrounded by Pilesgrove Township farmland: Victorian and colonial homes on the old streets around South Main, the Salem River's headwater ponds at the edge of town, and working farms starting at the borough line in every direction. Groundhogs are Woodstown's headline animal, digging under the borough's sheds and porches and throughout the surrounding fields. Raccoons take the older chimneys, bats the attics, and skunks make their February rounds of the whole town, one porch at a time.

Yard damage tells its own story. Groundhog burrows throw fans of excavated soil against foundations, skunks leave neat cone-shaped holes hunting grubs, and moles push ridges and mounds across lawns that were level in April. Treating the yard means reading which animal made which sign — the remedies differ completely — and fixing the conditions underneath: grub-heavy turf, brush piles, and woodpiles stacked against the house. Burrows at foundations get backfilled and screened once the animals are out; a hole simply filled with dirt is a hole an animal reopens in a night. Woodstown's yards end at farm fields, so the ground survey here reads the back lot line as part of the property, because that is where the burrows that matter are dug.

faqs.q: What should I do about a skunk under my Pittsgrove Township porch?
faqs.a: Keep dogs inside at dusk and do not try to block the opening while the skunk is home — that traps it and guarantees a spray. Our crew removes skunks from under porches and decks in Pittsgrove Township with covered, low-stress handling, then screens the opening so the next skunk cannot move in.

faqs.q: Are bats a problem in Pittsgrove Township homes?
faqs.a: Yes — older rooflines and quiet attics in Pittsgrove Township host summer colonies, and in Salem County the work is exclusion only, timed around the maternity season. Our crew maps every entry, fits one-way exits in the right window, and seals the building behind the bats.
